title: Austin Beutner Challenges Karen Bass for LA Mayor in 2026
text:
“`html
Austin Beutner Launches Mayoral Bid, Directly Challenging Karen Bass in 2026 Election
Los Angeles voters will have at least one clear choice in the June 2026 mayoral election, as former LAUSD Superintendent Austin Beutner officially announced his candidacy Monday, October 13th, wiht a video released on YouTube. The 65-year-old investment banker and philanthropist intends to unseat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass.
Beutner, who led the Los Angeles Unified school District from 2018 to 2021, framed his campaign as a defense of core values and a call for stronger leadership. “I’ll never accept the Trump administration’s assault on our values and our neighbors. Targeting people solely based on the color of their skin is unacceptable and un-American,” he stated in the announcement video.
However, the core of Beutner’s initial challenge centers on Bass’s handling of critical city issues, particularly crime and development. He has been especially critical of the administration’s response to January’s devastating Palisades Fire, alleging a “failure of leadership” as the blaze, fueled by strong winds, destroyed homes and businesses and tragically resulted in 12 fatalities.
The Bass campaign swiftly responded to Beutner’s entry into the race. A spokesperson for Mayor Bass, Doug Herman, asserted that the current administration has already made meaningful strides in addressing the city’s most pressing concerns. “When Karen Bass ran for mayor, homelessness and public safety were the top concerns of Angelenos. And she has delivered in a big way,” Herman stated monday morning. He highlighted a reported decrease in homelessness for two consecutive years, increased housing placements, and a decline in violent crime, including a drop in homicides to a 60-year low. “these achievements represent real progress for families in Los Angeles,” Herman continued.
The Palisades Fire hit particularly close to home for Beutner, as the blaze damaged his own property and destroyed his mother-in-law’s home. A recent after-action report from the LA Fire Department revealed systemic issues during the crisis, including poor interaction, inexperienced leadership, insufficient resources, and an ineffective firefighter recall process. Bass has as pledged to address these shortcomings.
Beutner was pointed in his criticism, stating, “When you have broken hydrants, a reservoir that’s broken and is out of action, broken [fire] trucks that you can’t dispatch ahead of time, when you don’t pre-deploy at the adequate level, when you don’t choose to hold over the Monday firefighters to be there on Tuesday to help fight the fire – to me, it’s a failure of leadership.” He concluded, “At the end of the day, the buck stops with the mayor.”
Bass’s office did not respond to a request for comment from city News Service.
Prior to his tenure at LAUSD, Beutner served as publisher of The Times from 2014-2015 and as a deputy mayor under former Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa from 2010-2013.
The 2026 mayoral race is already shaping up to be competitive, with developer Rick Caruso – who unsuccessfully challenged Bass in 2022 – also considered a potential candidate.Caruso, who also owns property in Pacific Palisades, has echoed Beutner’s criticisms of Bass’s leadership during the fire crisis, attributing the devastation to “incompetence, mismanagement and failure to plan, prepare and predeploy.”
Bass responded to Caruso’s remarks on Wednesday, expressing disappointment and suggesting his criticism was reminiscent of former President Trump. “Well,the way he characterized me sounded like Trump,” she said. “But I just was saddened by it, honestly, because that response was beneath him. This is when the city needs to stand together. Why would you do that? So he’s better than that and I was just disappointed and sad.”
